--- course-unit: ch04-jump-processes status: complete --- # Continuous-time Markov chains and jump processes Jump models are useful when the event itself is the object of interest. Instead of moving the SIR state a small distance at every numerical time step, we wait for the next infection or recovery and move the integer state by one. This is the continuous-time Markov-chain (CTMC) view of the epidemic. ## Learning goals By the end of this chapter, you should be able to: - translate SIR transitions into propensities and stoichiometric change vectors; - explain the Gillespie direct stochastic simulation algorithm (SSA); - construct a current Catalyst reaction network and simulate it with JumpProcesses; and - use population conservation and an ODE ensemble comparison as checks on a stochastic implementation. ## Model assumptions and classification We use the same closed, homogeneously mixing population as in the ODE chapter. There are \(N=1000\) people, with \(S(0)=990\), \(I(0)=10\), and \(R(0)=0\). Each infectious person makes \(c=10\) potentially infectious contacts per unit time, a contact transmits with probability \(\beta=0.05\), and an infectious person recovers at rate \(\gamma=0.25\). Recovered people do not return to the susceptible class; births, deaths, age structure, and imported infections are omitted. This is a **stochastic, continuous-time, discrete-state, population-level** model. It is population-level because the state records counts, not identities. It is a CTMC because, conditional on the current counts, the future does not depend on the earlier path. The two event types are | event | state change \(\boldsymbol{\nu}_j\) | propensity \(a_j(S,I,R)\) | |---|---|---| | infection \(S+I\to 2I\) | \((-1,+1,0)\) | \(a_1=\kappa SI\) | | recovery \(I\to R\) | \((0,-1,+1)\) | \(a_2=\gamma I\) | Here \(\kappa=\beta c/N\). The division by \(N\) makes the total infection rate comparable across population sizes: every susceptible has force of infection \(\beta cI/N\). ## Equations Let \(X(t)=(S(t),I(t),R(t))^\mathsf{T}\) and let \(Y_1,Y_2\) be independent unit-rate Poisson processes. The random time-change representation is $$ X(t)=X(0)+\boldsymbol{\nu}_1Y_1\!\left(\int_0^t a_1(X(s^-))\,ds\right) +\boldsymbol{\nu}_2Y_2\!\left(\int_0^t a_2(X(s^-))\,ds\right). $$ The left limit \(X(s^-)\) matters: the propensity is evaluated immediately before an event. Equivalently, if the current state is \(x\), the total event rate is \(a_0(x)=a_1(x)+a_2(x)\). The next waiting time is $$ \tau\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(a_0(x)), \qquad \Pr(J=j\mid x)=\frac{a_j(x)}{a_0(x)}. $$ This is the direct Gillespie algorithm [@gillespie1977]. Applying \(x\leftarrow x+\boldsymbol{\nu}_J\) and repeating gives an exact simulation of this CTMC (up to floating-point arithmetic). Taking expected changes per unit time gives the familiar mean-field equations, $$ \frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix}S\\I\\R\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-\kappa SI\\ \kappa SI-\gamma I\\ \gamma I\end{pmatrix}. $$ {#eq-jump-mean-field} Both the CTMC and Equation @eq-jump-mean-field conserve \(S+I+R=N\). The equality of their *means* is not exact at finite population size because nonlinear terms such as \(SI\) require a moment closure: \(\mathbb{E}[SI]\ne\mathbb{E}[S]\mathbb{E}[I]\). ## Julia implementation The course environment contains Catalyst 16.2.1 and JumpProcesses 9.29.1. The reaction network below is deliberately visible: its species are the coordinates of \(X\), and its reaction rates are the propensities above. Catalyst's current `JumpProblem` constructor creates the compatible JumpProcesses representation; `Direct()` selects Gillespie's direct aggregator and `SSAStepper()` advances from jump to jump. No fixed numerical step is used to define the event process. ::: {#cell-code-ch04-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using CairoMakie using Catalyst using JumpProcesses using OrdinaryDiffEq using StableRNGs using Statistics const N = 1000 const β = 0.05 const c = 10.0 const γ = 0.25 const κ = β * c / N const u₀ = [:S => 990, :I => 10, :R => 0] const tspan = (0.0, 40.0) const times = collect(0.0:0.2:40.0) sir_network = @reaction_network begin κ, S + I --> 2I γ, I --> R end ``` ::: {#code-ch04-setup .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
Model ##ReactionSystem#285:
Unknowns (3): see unknowns(##ReactionSystem#285)
  S(t)
  I(t)
  R(t)
Parameters (2): see parameters(##ReactionSystem#285)
  κ
  γ
``` ::: ::: ::: The symbols `κ` and `γ` in the network are parameters. The initial state is integer-valued because a half-person is not a valid CTMC state. We pass parameter values by name, which is safer than relying on the order of a positional vector. ::: {#cell-code-ch04-simulate .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} jump_parameters = [:κ => κ, :γ => γ] jump_problem = JumpProblem( sir_network, u₀, tspan, jump_parameters; aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(20250711), ) jump_solution = solve(jump_problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = times) jump_states = Array(jump_solution(times)) ``` ::: {#code-ch04-simulate .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3×201 Matrix{Int64}: 990 990 990 989 989 989 988 988 … 277 275 274 273 273 273 272 10 9 7 8 8 8 8 6 30 29 26 24 23 23 20 0 1 3 3 3 3 4 6 693 696 700 703 704 704 708 ``` ::: ::: The `JumpProblem` stores the CTMC and the random-number generator. Calling `solve` returns a piecewise-constant solution: the state changes at event times and remains unchanged between events. `saveat` samples that path for plotting; it does not turn the model into a time-stepped approximation. For comparison, the deterministic right-hand side uses exactly the drift in Equation @eq-jump-mean-field: ::: {#cell-code-ch04-ode-comparison .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function sir_drift!(du, u, p, t) κ, γ = p infection = κ * u[1] * u[2] recovery = γ * u[2] du[1] = -infection du[2] = infection - recovery du[3] = recovery return nothing end ode_problem = ODEProblem(sir_drift!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], tspan, (κ, γ)) ode_solution = solve(ode_problem, Tsit5(); saveat = times) ode_states = Array(ode_solution) ``` ::: {#code-ch04-ode-comparison .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3×201 Matrix{Float64}: 990.0 988.986 987.922 986.806 … 210.46 210.142 209.834 10.0 10.5017 11.0274 11.5781 15.3356 14.8978 14.472 0.0 0.512444 1.05057 1.6156 774.204 774.96 775.694 ``` ::: ::: The `ODEProblem` uses floating-point counts because it represents expected population flow, whereas the Catalyst problem uses integer species counts. Keeping the two constructors adjacent makes the code-to-equation mapping explicit. ::: {#cell-fig-ch04-jump-trajectories .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (760, 430)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "people", title = "Gillespie SIR path") labels = ["S (jump)", "I (jump)", "R (jump)"] colors = [:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen] for j in 1:3 stairs!(ax, times, jump_states[j, :]; color = colors[j], linewidth = 2, label = labels[j]) end lines!(ax, times, ode_states[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 2, label = "I (ODE)") axislegend(ax, position = :rt) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch04-jump-trajectories .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` One exact CTMC SIR trajectory and its deterministic mean-field comparison. ::: ::: ## Validation The first check is structural rather than statistical: every reaction changes one compartment down and another up. Thus conservation should hold at every saved point. ::: {#cell-code-ch04-conservation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} mass_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(jump_states; dims = 1)) .- N)) minimum_count = minimum(jump_states) @assert mass_error == 0 @assert minimum_count >= 0 (; mass_error, minimum_count, number_of_events = length(jump_solution.t) - 1) ``` ::: {#code-ch04-conservation .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (mass_error = 0, minimum_count = 0, number_of_events = 1626) ``` ::: ::: An individual path is not expected to lie on the ODE curve. A more informative check averages independent paths. Each repetition receives a fresh, deterministically chosen `StableRNG`, so the calculation is reproducible without changing Julia's global random state. ::: {#cell-code-ch04-ensemble .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function simulate_jump(seed) problem = JumpProblem( sir_network, u₀, tspan, jump_parameters; aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(seed), ) solution = solve(problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = times) return Array(solution(times)) end ensemble = cat((simulate_jump(3000 + k) for k in 1:16)...; dims = 3) ensemble_mean = dropdims(mean(ensemble; dims = 3), dims = 3) infectious_rmse = sqrt(mean((ensemble_mean[2, :] .- ode_states[2, :]).^2)) @assert maximum(abs.(sum(ensemble; dims = 1) .- N)) == 0 infectious_rmse ``` ::: {#code-ch04-ensemble .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 6.240473193802095 ``` ::: ::: With only 16 paths, the RMSE is a diagnostic rather than a precision estimate. Increasing the number of paths narrows Monte Carlo error approximately as \(1/\sqrt{M}\), but costs proportionally more simulations. ## Interpretation and limitations The CTMC retains integer counts and event timing, so it can represent extinction, early fade-out, and variability in the epidemic peak. Its propensities still assume homogeneous mixing and exponential recovery times. Real contact networks, latent periods, reporting delays, births, and time-varying interventions require additional states or a different model. For very large populations, exact SSA can spend most of its time processing events; tau-leaping, hybrid jump-ODE models, or an ODE may then be more appropriate, with an explicit approximation trade-off. The [JumpProcesses continuous-time tutorial](https://docs.sciml.ai/JumpProcesses/stable/tutorials/discrete_stochastic_example/) and [Catalyst documentation](https://docs.sciml.ai/Catalyst/stable/) document the APIs used here. The event formulation follows Gillespie's exact SSA [@gillespie1977] and the epidemic interpretation follows the original SIR model [@kermack1927]. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch04-ex1} Replace the recovery reaction by two sequential stages, \(I_1\to I_2\to R\), with rates \(2\gamma\) for both transitions. Add the fourth state to the Julia model, simulate 40 time units with a fixed seed, and verify both \(S+I_1+I_2+R=N\) and nonnegative integer states. Explain why two exponential stages have a less variable infectious duration than one exponential stage with mean \(1/\gamma\). ### Exercise 2 {#ch04-ex2} Use the low-level `ConstantRateJump(rate, affect!)` interface from JumpProcesses to implement a one-person birth-death toy process, then use the same direct-SSA ideas to add a vaccination jump \(S\to R\) to SIR. State the new propensity, update the ODE comparison, and discuss how a vaccination rate that depends on calendar time would change the jump type or simulation setup. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/04-jump-processes.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/04-jump-processes.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/04-jump-processes.jl)
